data.plain: Returning a number or conclusion from a computation whose preconditions failed, where a typed refusal was required.

analogy.boundary: The picture only covers the missing input; it says nothing about whether a dose worked out from complete inputs is right.

maps.analogy: the missing patient weight the dose formula needs
maps.doctrine: a precondition that does not hold

maps.analogy: guessing a dose and handing it over
maps.doctrine: returning a value anyway to keep going

maps.analogy: a written note saying 'dose not worked out: weight missing'
maps.doctrine: a typed refusal carrying its reason and evidence

analogy.text: A pharmacist guesses a dose when the patient's weight, the one input the formula needs, is missing, instead of saying the dose cannot be worked out yet.

reader.counterexample: A statistics routine returns a coefficient computed beyond its valid sample size, and a later summary reports it as a normal result because it arrived as a number.
reader.does_not_prove: A correct refusal in one place says nothing about whether the numbers this computation does return are right.

example.text: The finance forecast evaluation component returns a typed refusal when the forecast horizon reaches or exceeds the sample size, or when the statistics library it needs is unavailable, instead of reporting a number computed outside its valid range.

reader.governs: Computations that are only valid for some inputs.
reader.plain: The mistake of producing a number anyway when something the number depends on is missing, instead of saying 'I cannot answer this, and here is why'.
reader.potential_misread: That returning some number is more helpful than refusing, when a number produced from missing inputs is worse because it passes as usable.
reader.refuses: Returning a meaningless statistic, a silent NaN or a conclusion outside the valid range just to keep the pipeline passing.
reader.requires: A result type that returns Ok only when the declared precondition holds and otherwise a refusal carrying the reason and evidence.
reader.why_it_matters: A made-up number looks like a real one to every later step, while a refusal stops the bad value where it starts.
